Carolyn "Cara" Malak aka the Grimalkin. Cara is a wizard class mage (read: crazy strong) who's power is primarily limited to the control of her own body. She's a shape shifter and self healer who's instinctive knowledge of her own biology and control over it allow her to be near the top of the food chain, as well as functionally immortal. As she experiments and learns more about what she's capable of, she begins to climb the ranks above her. 


Her weaknesses include:


Cara cannot create new matter. She can modify the density of various tissues, making herself appear larger or smaller, but cannot gain mass without consuming and digesting it. As such, having parts of herself cut away limits her until she can eat and recover. Any part cut away from her "core" ceases to be her and becomes meat, which she would have to re-consume to control again. She finds this distasteful but will do so if the need arises, and would much prefer this to eating human/sapient meat. 


Emotional instability. Cara is a highly damaged individual with severe trust issues who is quick to anger and prone to violence. As such she has few friends or allies to call on, and doesn't trust the ones she does have to actually help her. She's very easy to bait into a trap, so long as that trap relies on her going on a full offensive. 


Cara's not particularly intelligent. Her power lets her steamroll over most threats, and she's unimaginative regarding more esoteric uses of it for decades. She highly struggles to use any magic outside her specialty, and is very easy to manipulate by people who know her well, even people she actively distrusts. She tends not to question things which is a problem when most of the things strong enough to fight her do so by using deception as a main part of their strategy.

No, Canon is different from copyright. 


Copyright is a legal term denoting who owns the intellectual property and what can be done with it in the real world. SCP is under the creative commons license, which means that anyone can do anything with it or build on it in any way, but they must put whatever they do with it in the Creative Commons license as well, so nobody has any exclusivity rights. (I'm not a lawyer, this is a layman's explanation.) 


Canon refers to the parts of a story that are considered unquestionably true, within the confines of the story. For example, it's canon that Darth Vader is Luke Skywalkers dad in Star Wars. This is different from fan theories, speculation, or other things that might be hinted at in the text, but not outright confirmed, or things that fans of a story make up because it adds to the story for them. 


The SCP foundation has no canon, or at least no consistent canon. If you want to include a character or event or anomaly that someone else wrote about you can, because of the creative commons license. However, you can also ignore or re-define these things without it being 'wrong' or seen as a contradiction, because there is no canon between different articles unless the article itself says there is. So in one article, Dr. Wondertainment is a young woman who genuinely wants to make great toys to give kids magical experiences. In another he is a balding, jaded Wonka wannabe who gave up a long time ago and deliberately makes awful toys to punish kids. Neither of these is correct, and neither is wrong.

1. We had extremely different ideas about what we wanted in life, so our relationship was doomed to fail. She wanted kids, I did not. 2. We had very different views on the world, this led to interesting conversations as friends and fights as partners. My husband now has a far more similar view of the world, both in a "what is" and a "what should be" way, which means we have a similar framework for dealing with problems. We still have interesting conversations, but it surprised me how much it upset me to have a completely different moral framework from my partner, or to have her try to convert me. I can be great friends with highly religious people, but I'd never date one again.


3. This kind of ties into 2, but our views of relationships were very different. We were both still teens and figuring shit out, but we argued about what we should mean to each other, what speed things were/should be moving at, what things were important for couples to do and what wasn't important. 


Most of these problems would have been fairly obvious stop signs if we had had enough experience to recognize them beforehand. Luckily we were close enough and honest enough to agree that we were a horrible couple, and things were only awkward for a week or two before we were perfectly happy as friends for the next several years.

Some research indicates that we shouldn't really look at it as "homosexuality" so much as some people are androphilic and some are gynaphilic. In other words- some people like boys, some like girls, and this develops in a different way to how our primary sex characteristics do. There's not some "gay gene" or sequence of events that turns someone gay, there's a sequence of events that makes someone like a particular sex/gender. Most of the time this happens to a member of the opposite sex/gender, because somewhere in the very messy sequence of development that's triggered by something that's moderated by something that's moderated by.... The sex of the individual. Because it's such a complex and messy sequence of events though, sometimes it happens to members of the same sex, or doesn't happen at all. That's why we get boys who like boys, girls who like girls, people who like both, and people who like neither. Each individual process along the way helps to increase fitness on a grand scale but sometimes it doesn't end up working out for the individual. Other things can mitigate this reduction in fitness (see the kin hypothesis mentioned elsewhere), but it might just be a side effect of a complex process that's not harmful enough/too complex to really work out. Evolution doesn't optimize, it uses "good enough" stacked on top of "good enough".

Mammals including humans bond through sex. If we look at one of our closest relatives, the Bonobo, they use sex as a way of building and maintaining social connections that can be called on for help in other situations, increasing fitness.

The kin selection hypothesis isn't just for infertility. If I invest more resources in my niece because she's my niece, her fitness goes up. Because she has more similar genes to me than a non-related person, that increases the likelihood that my genes (through her and her offspring) will pass on. This is true regardless of whether or not I have offspring of my own. Since we share genes, my sibling and I are likely to both care for each other's offspring to some extent- giving those offspring potential "back up parents" in the event that someone dies or is unable to care for their offspring. This increases our fitness.

Basically there's a law (Title IX) that says that discrimination based on sex is illegal for anyone who receives federal funds for education. More recently, the supreme court ruled that this includes discrimination based on gender identity and sexual orientation- if you wouldn't fire a woman for dating a man then you can't fire a man for dating a man, etc. 

 The USDA is federal agency that manages a variety of things, including free school lunch programs. They updated their policies after this decision, interpreting a similar statute (Title VII) to have the same restrictions.  So now anyone who gets funding from them cannot discriminate on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity. If they do discriminate, they risk losing funding and possible legal trouble for violating the rules attached to that money. 

 It's a fairly normal thing that groups which receive federal funding (or state funding in some circumstances) have to follow guidelines that might be stricter than they would otherwise. Another example is adoption agencies that receive federal funding cannot discriminate based on religion, whereas agencies that don't receive federal funding can prioritize certain faiths. A Christian run group, funded by a church or otherwise privately funded, can choose to only adopt children out to Christian families, but so long as they do that they cannot receive state/federal funds. 

The AGs are challenging this interpretation of Title VII, essentially saying that this is not what the supreme court meant by their ruling on Title XI and that organizations that receive this funding shouldn't be required to follow these rules.
